sections.title: About you and the property
sections.blurb: Most of this we fill in for you. Just check it.

sections.title: Disputes
sections.blurb: Any fallings-out about the property or a neighbour.

sections.title: Notices
sections.blurb: Letters or plans that affect your property or the area.

sections.title: Changes to the property
sections.blurb: Building work, windows, solar panels, listed status.

sections.title: Guarantees and warranties
sections.blurb: Paperwork that still protects the work done.

sections.blurb: Shared drives, paths, drains, pipes and cables.

questions.q: Is this the correct address for the property you are selling?
questions.help: We have taken this from your solicitor's file and HM Land Registry. Tell us if anything looks wrong.

questions.q: What is the property's Unique Property Reference Number (UPRN)?
questions.help: Optional. It is a public ID for the building. We normally find this for you, so you can skip it.

questions.q: Please confirm the full name of every legal owner, exactly as it appears on the title deeds.
questions.help: Every owner named on the title has to answer and sign this form. Middle names included.

questions.q: What is your role in the sale?
questions.help: If you are selling on behalf of someone else - for example after a death, or under a power of attorney - pick that option and we will ask for the paperwork.

evidence.label: Grant of probate, power of attorney or trust deed
evidence.hint: A photo of the first page is enough to start with.

questions.q: When did you become the owner, or get the authority to sell?
questions.help: Roughly is fine if you cannot remember the exact day - we can check it against the title register.

questions.q: Is the owner a company rather than a person?
questions.help: Only tick yes if the registered owner is a limited company or similar.

followUp.q: Please give the company number, country of incorporation, and the name of the director or authorised person signing.

questions.q: Standing on the road looking at your home - who looks after the boundary on the LEFT?
questions.help: Boundary means the fence, wall, hedge or ditch. If you have always repaired it, that usually means it is yours. Not known is a perfectly acceptable answer.

questions.q: And the boundary on the RIGHT?
questions.help: Same question, other side. Still looking from the road.

questions.q: And at the REAR (the back)?
questions.help: The boundary at the far end of the garden.

questions.q: And at the FRONT?
questions.help: The boundary between your property and the road or pavement.

questions.q: Are your boundaries an unusual shape, so that left, right, front and back does not really describe them?
questions.help: For example a corner plot, a wedge shape, or a garden that wraps around another house.

followUp.q: Describe who owns which boundary. A rough sketch photo works too.

evidence.label: Sketch or plan marking the boundaries
evidence.hint: Print the title plan, draw on it, photograph it.

questions.q: Has any boundary been moved, or land added or taken, while you have owned the property?
questions.help: Includes a neighbour building on or fencing off part of your land, or you taking in a piece of spare ground.

followUp.q: What changed, roughly when, and was anything agreed in writing?

questions.q: Does any part of your property stick out over, or run under, the boundary?
questions.help: Classic examples: a cellar under the pavement, overhanging eaves or guttering, a covered walkway, a bay window over the path.

followUp.q: Please describe what overhangs or runs underneath.

questions.q: Has a Party Wall notice ever been served, by you or on you?
questions.help: A formal letter about work on a shared wall or close to a boundary - usually headed Party Wall etc. Act 1996. If you had a loft conversion or extension next to a neighbour, there may be one.

followUp.q: Which boundary did it relate to, and was the work carried out?

evidence.label: Party wall notice or award

questions.q: Have there been any disputes or complaints about your property, or one nearby?
questions.help: Be straight with this one. It covers noise, parking, pets, boundaries, building work, anti-social behaviour - whether or not solicitors got involved. Buyers can claim compensation later if it is hidden.

followUp.q: What happened, roughly when, who was involved, and is it settled?

questions.q: Is anything simmering that could turn into a dispute after you have moved?
questions.help: For example a neighbour unhappy about your extension, an ongoing disagreement about a shared drive, or a complaint you have made that has not been resolved.

followUp.q: Please explain the situation.

questions.q: Have you had, or sent, any letters or notices that affect the property or one nearby?
questions.help: From a neighbour, the council, a government department or a utility. Includes planning application letters through the door, enforcement notices, and road scheme consultations.

followUp.q: What was it about, who sent it, and roughly when?

evidence.label: Copy of the notice or letter

questions.q: Do you know of any plans to build on or develop land nearby?
questions.help: New housing on a nearby field, a phone mast, a solar farm, a road scheme. Only what you actually know about - you are not expected to research it.

followUp.q: What is proposed and where?

questions.q: Do you know of any plans to alter or change the use of buildings nearby?
questions.help: For example a house nearby becoming flats, a shop becoming a takeaway, or a pub being converted.

followUp.q: What is proposed and where?

questions.q: Which of these has been done to the property? Tick everything you know about, even if it was before your time.
opts: Replacement windows, roof windows, roof lights or glazed doors (since April 2002)
questions.help: Tick from what you know. We will only ask for detail on what you tick. Gas and electrical work comes later, in the Services section.

questions.q: For the work you ticked - what was done and roughly when? Not known is a valid answer for anything before you owned it.
questions.help: One line each is plenty. For example: rear extension, about 2014, built by a local builder.

questions.q: Has all of that work been finished?
questions.help: Finished means completed, not necessarily signed off by the council - we ask about paperwork next.

followUp.q: What is still to be done?

questions.q: Do you have the paperwork for that work - planning permission, building regulations completion certificate, or a FENSA or CERTASS certificate for windows?
questions.help: This is the single biggest cause of delay in a sale. If you cannot find it, say so now and we will order copies from the council for you rather than waiting until the buyer's solicitor asks.

evidence.label: Planning permission, building regs certificate, FENSA or CERTASS certificate
evidence.hint: Photos of each certificate. Blurry is fine as long as we can read the reference.

questions.q: Was any of that work done while you owned the property?
questions.help: This matters because you may have needed consent from a freeholder, a management company, or under a covenant on the title.

questions.q: Is any part of the property used only for business, not as a home?
questions.help: Working from home at the kitchen table does not count. A room converted into a salon, surgery, shop or let-out office does.

followUp.q: What is the use, and which part of the property?

evidence.label: Any planning permission for that use

questions.q: As far as you know, has anything been built or changed without the permission it needed?
questions.help: For example an extension with no building regs sign-off, or a condition on a planning permission that was never met. Saying so now is far cheaper than it surfacing during the sale - it can usually be fixed with indemnity insurance.

followUp.q: Please explain what you know.

questions.q: Is there any outstanding planning or building control issue you know needs sorting out?
questions.help: An open enforcement case, a certificate never issued, an inspection never finished.

followUp.q: Please give details.

questions.q: Are there solar panels on the property?
questions.help: Panels for electricity, hot water or heating. If no, we skip the next eight questions.

questions.q: Are the panels only for hot water or heating, rather than generating electricity?
questions.help: Solar thermal panels heat water. Photovoltaic (PV) panels make electricity. If you get money back for generating power, they are PV.

questions.q: Which year were they installed?
questions.help: Approximately is fine.

questions.q: Do you own the panels outright?
questions.help: Some older installations were free in exchange for leasing your roof to the installer. That matters a lot to a buyer's mortgage lender.

questions.q: Has a long lease of the roof or air space been granted to a solar company?
questions.help: Typically 20 to 25 years. If you are not sure, say no and we will check the title for you.

evidence.label: Roof lease

questions.q: Is there a maintenance agreement for the system?

evidence.label: Maintenance agreement

questions.q: Is there a battery storing the solar power?

followUp.q: What make, model and size (kWh) is the battery? A photo of its label will do.

questions.q: Does the system feed electricity back into the grid?
questions.help: If you receive payments for exporting power, the answer is yes.

questions.q: Is there a Feed-in Tariff (FIT) or Smart Export Guarantee (SEG) in place?
questions.help: These are the schemes that pay you for the power you generate or export. A buyer will want the agreement transferred.

evidence.label: FIT or SEG agreement plus a recent electricity bill showing the credit

questions.q: Do you have the installation certificate for the panels (usually MCS)?
questions.help: MCS certification is often needed for the export payments to transfer to the buyer.

evidence.label: MCS or equivalent installation certificate

questions.q: Is the property, or any part of it, a listed building?
questions.help: We check the national register for you, so just confirm what we found. Listing can cover a wall, gate or outbuilding as well as the house.

questions.q: Is the property in a conservation area?
questions.help: We look this up from the council's data, so just confirm.

questions.q: Are any trees on or overhanging the property protected by a Tree Preservation Order (TPO)?
questions.help: A TPO means you need council permission before pruning or felling. We check the council register where it is published.

followUp.q: Has any work been done to those trees? If so, what and when?

evidence.label: The TPO and any consent for tree work

questions.q: Which of these guarantees or warranties are still running on the property? Tick what you have.
opts: Windows, roof lights or glazed doors
questions.help: Unexpired means it still has time left to run. Have a look in the folder where you keep house paperwork - we will ask for copies of whatever you tick.

evidence.label: The guarantee or warranty documents you ticked

questions.q: What is the other guarantee for?
Have you ever claimed on any of them?

followUp.q: What was the claim, when, and how did it end?

questions.q: Has anything been done that might invalidate one of them?
questions.help: For example a damp proof guarantee that requires annual inspections that stopped happening, or DIY work on a system still under warranty.

followUp.q: Please explain.

questions.q: Do you insure the building yourself?
questions.help: If it is a flat or on an estate, the freeholder or management company often insures the building instead of you.

followUp.q: Who insures it?

questions.q: Has buildings insurance ever been refused, loaded with a high excess, or gone up sharply because of the property itself?
questions.help: Usually flood, subsidence or a past claim. A general price rise at renewal does not count. This tells the buyer whether they will be able to insure it.

followUp.q: Please give details.

questions.q: Have you made any buildings insurance claims?
questions.help: Escape of water, storm damage, subsidence, fire, accidental damage.

followUp.q: What for, when, and how was it resolved?

questions.q: Has any part of the property, including the garden, ever flooded? Tick any that apply.
opts: Yes - from a river or the sea
Yes - from surface water or run-off after heavy rain
Yes - from a burst pipe, drain or sewer
questions.help: Water in the garden, garage or under the floorboards counts, not just water in the living room. We already have the Environment Agency flood risk rating for the postcode - this is about what has actually happened.

followUp.q: When did it flood, how deep did the water get, and what was done afterwards?

questions.q: Has a flood risk report or assessment been obtained for the property?

evidence.label: Flood risk report

questions.q: Has the property ever been tested for radon gas?
questions.help: Radon is a natural gas that collects in some buildings, mainly in parts of the South West, Derbyshire and Northamptonshire. We can tell you from the postcode whether it is a radon area.

followUp.q: Was the result below the recommended action level?

evidence.label: Radon test report

questions.q: Has any work been done to reduce radon levels?
questions.help: Usually a sump and fan, or a membrane fitted during building work.

questions.q: Is there a Green Deal loan attached to the electricity bill?
questions.help: A government scheme where energy improvements were paid for through the electricity bill. The debt passes to the buyer, so it has to be declared. If you have never heard of it, the answer is almost certainly no.

followUp.q: What was installed under the scheme?

evidence.label: Latest electricity bill showing the Green Deal charge

questions.q: Is the property affected by Japanese knotweed?
questions.help: A fast-spreading plant with bamboo-like stems and heart-shaped leaves that lenders take seriously. If you are not sure, answer not known and send us a photo of the plant - we will identify it.

followUp.q: Is there a treatment plan in place?

evidence.label: Treatment plan and any linked insurance cover

questions.q: Has a Japanese knotweed survey been done?

evidence.label: Knotweed survey

questions.q: Do you use any part of a neighbour's land, or share anything with them?
questions.help: A shared drive, a path across next door's garden to your bins, a jointly used yard, parking on land that is not yours, a septic tank in a neighbour's field.

followUp.q: What do you use, and whose land is it?

questions.q: Do you pay towards the upkeep of anything shared?

followUp.q: How much, how often, and who do you pay?

questions.q: Has there ever been a disagreement about it?

followUp.q: Please give details.

questions.q: Does anyone else have the right to come onto your land, or use part of it?
questions.help: A neighbour crossing your drive, a shared bin store, a right to maintain their wall from your side, a farmer with access to a field.

followUp.q: Who, and what do they use?

questions.q: Have you asked them to contribute to the cost of maintaining it?

followUp.q: How much, how often, and does it come to you or to someone else?

questions.q: Any disagreement about that arrangement?

followUp.q: Please give details.

questions.q: Do any drains, pipes or cables serving your home run across someone else's land?
questions.help: Not known is completely normal here - most people have no idea. Your solicitor can check the drainage plan.

questions.q: And do any serving other properties run across yours?
questions.help: A neighbour's drain or water pipe crossing your garden, for example.

questions.q: Is there any written agreement about those drains, pipes or cables?

evidence.label: The agreement, or a note of what was agreed

questions.q: Where do cars park at the property?
questions.help: Tick everything that applies.

questions.q: Do you need a council permit to park on the road?
questions.help: A resident's permit scheme or controlled parking zone.

questions.q: Is there an electric vehicle charging point?
What type of charger and connector is it, and where is it fitted? A photo of the unit is ideal.

evidence.label: EV charger building regulations or electrical approval

questions.q: Does the charging cable have to cross the public pavement?
questions.help: If the car is on the road and the charger is on the house, the cable crosses the pavement - councils usually require a licence.

followUp.q: Is there a council licence or agreement for it?

questions.q: Has any electrical work been done at the property, as far as you know?
questions.help: A new consumer unit or fuse box, rewiring, new sockets, outside lighting, a shower, a hot tub supply.

followUp.q: What was done and roughly when?

questions.q: Do you have a certificate from the electrician for that work?
questions.help: An electrical installation certificate, minor works certificate, or a Part P building regulations compliance certificate.

evidence.label: Electrical certificate for the work

questions.q: Is there an Electrical Installation Condition Report (EICR)?
questions.help: A periodic inspection report on the whole electrical system, usually a multi-page document with lots of ticks and codes. Landlords must have one; owner-occupiers often do not.

evidence.label: EICR

questions.q: How is the property heated? Tick all that apply.

followUp.q: What is the other heating?

questions.q: When was the heating system installed?
questions.help: Not known is fine - and common if it was in before you moved in.

questions.q: When was the boiler installed?
questions.help: Sometimes written on a sticker inside the boiler door or in the service record.

questions.q: Has the heating system been replaced, other than swapping the boiler?
questions.help: New radiators throughout, underfloor heating put in, a switch from one fuel to another.

questions.q: Do you have the installation or commissioning paperwork for the heating (for gas, a Gas Safe building regulations notification)?

evidence.label: Heating installation or commissioning certificate

questions.q: Is the heating and hot water working properly right now?

followUp.q: What is wrong with it?

questions.q: Which year was it last serviced?
questions.help: A photo of the service sticker on the boiler or the last invoice answers this and gives us the certificate at the same time.

evidence.label: Latest service report
evidence.hint: Photograph the sticker inside the boiler door.

questions.q: Is there more than one heating system?
questions.help: For example gas central heating plus a woodburner, or a separate system in an annexe.

followUp.q: Tell us about the other system - what it is, when it went in, and when it was last serviced.

questions.q: Is the property connected to mains drainage for toilets and waste water?
questions.help: Most homes are. If you have a septic tank, the answer is no.

questions.q: And for rainwater from the roof and drives?
questions.help: Not known is very common. Some homes drain rainwater into a soakaway in the garden instead.

questions.q: Is waste water dealt with by any of these?
opts: None of these - it all goes to mains sewer
questions.help: If everything goes into the mains sewer, pick the last option and we will skip ten questions.

questions.q: When did the system start being used?

showIf.notOnly: None of these - it all goes to mains sewer

questions.q: When was it installed?

showIf.notOnly: None of these - it all goes to mains sewer

questions.q: When was it last replaced or upgraded?

showIf.notOnly: None of these - it all goes to mains sewer

questions.q: When was the cesspool last emptied?
When was the treatment plant last serviced?

evidence.label: Service record for the treatment plant

questions.q: Where does the treated water end up?
opts: Into the ground (drainage field or soakaway)
Into a stream, ditch or other surface water

showIf.notOnly: None of these - it all goes to mains sewer

questions.help: This decides which environmental rules apply. Not known is acceptable.

questions.q: Has the system been replaced or upgraded since January 2020, or does it meet the General Binding Rules?

showIf.notOnly: None of these - it all goes to mains sewer

questions.help: Rules changed in 2020 for systems discharging to surface water. If you do not know, say so - your solicitor will look into it.

questions.q: Do other properties share the system?

showIf.notOnly: None of these - it all goes to mains sewer

followUp.q: How many properties share it, who manages it, and how are the costs split?

questions.q: Is any part of the system, or the way you get to it, outside your boundary?

showIf.notOnly: None of these - it all goes to mains sewer

evidence.label: Plan showing where the system is and how you reach it

questions.q: Do you have a permit or any paperwork for the system?

showIf.notOnly: None of these - it all goes to mains sewer

evidence.label: Environment Agency permit or registration, installation paperwork

questions.q: Mains electricity - who supplies it, and where is the meter?

fields.label: MPAN number
fields.hint: A long number on your bill, sometimes labelled Supply Number. Skip it if you cannot see it - a photo of the bill is easier.

questions.help: The quickest way to answer this whole section: photograph your latest electricity bill and we will read the supplier and MPAN off it.

evidence.label: Latest electricity bill
evidence.hint: One photo answers most of this.

questions.q: Mains gas - who supplies it, and where is the meter?

fields.label: MPRN number
fields.hint: On your gas bill. Skip if you cannot find it.

evidence.label: Latest gas bill

questions.q: Mains water - who supplies it, and where is the stopcock?

fields.label: Where is the stopcock?
fields.hint: Usually under the kitchen sink or in a downstairs cupboard.

fields.label: Where is the water meter, if there is one?

questions.help: We can work out your water company from the postcode, so mostly we just need the stopcock location - which buyers genuinely want to know.

questions.q: Mains sewerage - who is the provider?
Small sewage treatment plant - details
Shared ground or air source heat pump - details
Phone and broadband - who are the providers?
questions.help: Buyers care about this more than almost anything else on the form. We also check the available speeds at your postcode and include them.

questions.q: Any other services connected - LPG, district heating, a private water supply?
Does this sale depend on you completing a purchase on the same day?
questions.help: In other words, are you in a chain - buying as well as selling?

questions.q: Do you have any particular requirements about the moving date?
questions.help: School terms, a job start date, a holiday booked, needing a specific day of the week. Tell us now and it can be built into the timetable.

followUp.q: What do you need?

questions.q: Do you live at the property?
Does anyone else aged 17 or over live there?
questions.help: Adult children, a partner not on the deeds, a parent, a lodger, a tenant.

questions.q: What are their full names?
Are any of them your tenants or lodgers?
Is any part of the property let out under a tenancy that is not being sold with it?
questions.help: For example an annexe or a flat above that stays let after the sale.

questions.q: Has everyone aged 17 or over agreed to sign the contract and move out on or before completion?
questions.help: Buyers' lenders insist on this. Anyone adult living there needs to confirm they are leaving.

questions.q: The property is not being sold empty - please send the tenancy details.

evidence.label: Tenancy agreements and details of every occupier

questions.q: Is there a mortgage on the property that will be paid off when you sell?
Will you clear all rubbish - including from the loft, garden, shed, garage and outbuildings - and leave the property clean and tidy?
questions.help: This is a promise to the buyer, not a trick question. Worth reading now rather than discovering it on moving day.

questions.q: Will everything included in the sale be left in the condition listed on the fittings and contents form?
questions.help: Carpets, curtains, white goods, light fittings - whatever you have said is included.

questions.q: Will anything you are taking with you, including anything fixed in place, be removed without leaving damage?
questions.help: If you are taking a wall-mounted TV bracket, a shed or a favourite shrub, it should come out cleanly - or be left.

questions.q: Will you leave all keys, plus codes for alarms and any other equipment, at the property or with the agent?
questions.help: Window keys, garage keys, meter cupboard keys, alarm codes, boiler app logins, EV charger app.

questions.q: Last paperwork request - do you have any written consents for the things you have told us about?
questions.help: Consents under covenants on the title, or from an estate management company or freeholder, for the building work, Green Deal, EV charger or services you mentioned. If you have none, tell us and we will check whether any were needed.

evidence.label: Consents under covenants or from a management company or freeholder

questions.q: Anything else a buyer ought to know that we have not asked about?
questions.help: Optional, but this is your chance. Noisy neighbours, a leak you have fixed, a planning application you are aware of, a quirk of the house. Telling the buyer now protects you from a claim later.
